findings.evidence: "A copy of each update goes to the shared benefits folder the same day." appears verbatim at the end of both the reimbursement-log paragraph and the equipment-catalog paragraph
findings.fix: Either confirm both processes really share this exact distribution step, or rewrite the second paragraph's closing sentence to describe its own distribution process distinctly.
findings.violation: The identical sentence is copy-pasted for two different artifacts, suggesting the second paragraph was cloned from the first without being tailored, and adding no new information.

findings.evidence: Three different owners (IT asset group, finance liaison, benefits team) and two different cadences (monthly vs. start of fiscal year) are given for maintaining the same equipment catalog.
findings.fix: Designate a single owner and a single update cadence for the equipment catalog, and remove or reconcile the duplicate statements.
findings.location: Program Overview, second paragraph ("the IT asset group tracks the equipment catalog on the first business day of the month") vs. Special Cases ("The finance liaison publishes the equipment catalog at the start of the fiscal year") vs. Questions and Updates ("The benefits team reviews the equipment catalog at the start of the fiscal year")
findings.violation: The document contradicts itself about who owns the equipment catalog and how often it is updated.

findings.evidence: "The stipend clock resumes on their first day back."
findings.fix: Name the specific clock (e.g., "the 90-day service requirement") instead of the undefined term "stipend clock."
findings.violation: "Stipend clock" is never defined - it's unclear whether this refers to the 90-day service requirement, the benefit-year claim limit, or something else.

findings.evidence: "The manager reviews the request within two business days." followed by "The requester gets an automatic reminder after three days."
findings.fix: Use consistent units (business days throughout) and clarify what constitutes a "missing item" that would make a request incomplete.
findings.violation: The timeline mixes "business days" and plain "days" inconsistently, and it's unclear what "the missing item" refers to since no prior section describes an item that could be missing from a request.

findings.evidence: "A photo of the receipt is enough for most requests."
findings.fix: Either state that a photo is always sufficient, or list the criteria/categories that require additional proof.
findings.violation: "Most requests" implies some requests require more than a photo, but the policy never specifies which ones or what additional documentation they need.

findings.evidence: "You must keep your equipment in good working condition and we may ask for a brief photo check once a year."
findings.fix: Rewrite in third person for consistency, e.g., "Employees must keep equipment in good working condition; the benefits team may request a brief photo check once a year."
findings.violation: This sentence switches to second-person voice ("you," "we") while every other section uses third-person voice ("employees," "the stipend," "the manager").

findings.evidence: "Similarly, the policy applies to one device per category per employee."
findings.fix: Replace "Similarly" with a neutral transition or move this sentence to sit next to the related claim-limit language in Eligibility.
findings.violation: "Similarly" implies this sentence supports or parallels the previous one about photo checks, but the one-device-per-category rule is an unrelated claim limit, not a similar restriction.

findings.evidence: "You record the stipend item on the request form. Finance reconciles the stipend item against the request log each month. Payroll releases the stipend item amount after that monthly review."
findings.fix: Rename the section to reflect its actual content (e.g., "Reconciliation Process") or replace the body with an actual glossary of terms used elsewhere in the policy.
findings.violation: The section is titled "Terminology Notes" but contains no definitions of terms - it's a process narrative, and it again lapses into second-person voice.

findings.fix: Identify a single responsible party and a single timeline for releasing/depositing reimbursement funds, and use consistent terminology across sections.
findings.location: Terminology Notes ("Payroll releases the stipend item amount after that monthly review") vs. Reimbursement Amounts ("The finance office deposits the amount within one pay cycle")
findings.violation: Two different actors (Payroll vs. finance office) and two different timings (after monthly reconciliation vs. within one pay cycle) are given for the same disbursement step.

findings.evidence: "Also, you submit the request in the portal. You track its status there until the payment clears."
findings.fix: Remove this redundant sentence or merge it into the "How to Apply" section where portal submission is already described.
findings.violation: This duplicates ground already covered in "How to Apply" without adding new information, and appears under an unrelated heading.

findings.evidence: "Completing the request begins with confirming eligibility, and uploading the receipt." vs. "The summary shows the equipment cost and the requested delivery date."
findings.fix: Clarify the actual order of operations (request/approval before purchase, or purchase before request) and make both sections consistent with it.
findings.location: Request Steps vs. How to Apply
findings.violation: Requiring a receipt to complete the request implies the purchase already happened, but the confirmation summary showing a "requested delivery date" implies the equipment has not yet been purchased/delivered - these two descriptions of the request process contradict each other on sequencing.

findings.evidence: "The finance liaison publishes the equipment catalog at the start of the fiscal year."
findings.fix: Either move this sentence to the Program Overview section where catalog maintenance is discussed, or replace this section with actual special-case content, and resolve the conflicting ownership noted above.
findings.violation: The heading "Special Cases" promises an exception or edge case, but the content is just another (conflicting) restatement of catalog-publishing ownership/timing, not a special case.

findings.evidence: "Once approved, the team schedules the reimbursement for the next pay cycle."
findings.fix: Consolidate the payment-processing narrative into one section with one clearly defined responsible party.
findings.violation: This introduces a third actor (the benefits team) responsible for reimbursement scheduling, on top of the finance office (Reimbursement Amounts) and Payroll (Terminology Notes), without reconciling who actually pays out the stipend.

findings.evidence: "The finance office also flags any request that repeats within the same quarter."
findings.fix: Clarify what "repeats" means (e.g., a duplicate submission of the same claim, or a different employee at the same address) or remove this rule if it conflicts with the one-claim-per-year limit.
findings.violation: This implies an employee could submit multiple requests within a quarter, but Eligibility states the stipend "covers one claim per employee per benefit year," so a repeat request within the same quarter should not be possible under the stated rules.

findings.evidence: "The finance office reviews every stipend request over 200 dollars before it pays out."
findings.fix: Integrate this finance-office review step into the Approval Timeline so the full approval sequence (manager review, then finance review if over $200) is described in one place.
findings.violation: Given the maximum stipend is 500 dollars, this threshold applies to most requests, yet this additional review step is never mentioned in the Approval Timeline section describing the request/approval process.

findings.fix: Explicitly state how the one-claim-per-year limit relates to the one-device-per-category limit (e.g., "a claim may include one device per category, up to the annual cap").
findings.location: Eligibility ("one claim per employee per benefit year") vs. Restrictions and Exceptions ("the policy applies to one device per category per employee")
findings.violation: It's ambiguous whether a single "claim" can include multiple devices across categories, or whether each device/category requires its own claim - the two limits aren't reconciled.
